# Writing practice

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
```

How does a question about your data turn into a sentence? Reading was
recognition; writing is recall. Psychologists use those two words for two kinds
of remembering. Recognition starts from something in front of you, and asks only
whether you have seen it before. That is what [Reading practice](reading.qmd)
did: it gave you finished sentences and asked what they say. Recall starts from
nothing in front of you: you produce the answer yourself. It is the harder of
the two, and it is what writing a sentence asks of you.

From here on, this chapter asks you to recall. Three worked examples come first.
The first two show the method you will use: start with the minimum sentence,
look, refine. The third asks you to write the whole sentence at once. Five
questions follow, each answered by a sentence you met in Reading practice. For
each, write your sentence before you look at the printed one, then check it. Last comes the other half of writing: what happens when a
sentence is wrong, and what a refusal tells you to do next.

## Which continents live longest? {#which-continents-live-longest}

This is the first of the three worked examples. Before reading on, try to
write the sentence that answers the question above: which mark, which
transform, which positions? Then build it one step at a time. Start with the
minimum sentence, the smallest one that shows the data:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life."* The plot shows
how each continent's countries spread, but the question asked for a comparison
of *typical* values, and this one shows every country. Swap `point` for `bar`, and attach the transform `mean`
with `*`; everything else stays:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life."* Now
there is one bar per continent, as tall as the mean life expectancy of its
countries.

Bars are easiest to compare when they are sorted, with the largest first. A
categorical column can carry a fixed order, declared when the table is built
([Declaring the order of categories](data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories)).
The order you want here depends on the means the plot has just computed, so the
table cannot carry it. The sentence has to ask for it: `order(life)` sorts the axis
by the bars' values for `life`, here the means, and `desc = TRUE` puts the
largest first:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  order(life, desc = TRUE)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, ordered
by life, largest first."*

That took two changes: `point` became `bar * mean`, and `order()` was added.
Neither rewrote the sentence. Each added or swapped words and left the rest in
place, and every word you kept still means the same thing.

## How do petal lengths differ by species? {#how-do-petal-lengths-differ-by-species}

Reading practice drew the first two plots below. Write the two sentences from
memory: the one-variable question first, then the same question split by
species.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length."* Now split
the same bars by species, with one word.

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species."*

If the overlapping bars are hard to compare, one mark changes that: `step`
draws each bin's height as an outline with no fill, so the three species never cover
each other:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by bin, x is petal length, color by
species."*

The transform never changed. `bin` cut the same intervals all three times. What
changed was first `color(species)`, which split the bars by species, and then
the mark that draws them. A transform you
learn once works with every mark that can take it.

## Where is the world's wealth, and its health? {#where-is-the-worlds-wealth-and-its-health}

The first two questions were each about one measurement. This one is about two,
income and life expectancy, and they fill both positions. Someone reading the plot also
wants to know how many people live in each country. [A first plot](first-plot.qmd)
built this sentence, without `size`, step by step. Write the whole sentence now, adding `size` for
population, then check:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
continent, size by population."* Three atoms were added to the minimum
sentence: `color`, `size` and `title`. The log scale is written inside `x`, so it
adds no word, and the sentence uses no word that the first chapter and the
grammar chapter have not shown.

## Five questions: write first, then check {#five-questions-nothing-in-front-of-you}

Each question below matches one plot from Reading practice. Write your
sentence first; the printed one is there to check against, not to read first.

Which countries won the most gold? Every country name has to stay readable,
so the bars should be horizontal.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(medals)
```

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country)
```

*"Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country."* Compared with the
first plot in Reading practice, the two bindings were swapped: `gold` on `x`, `country` on `y`. That makes the bars horizontal,
and no new word was needed.

How is life expectancy distributed, drawn as a smooth curve rather than
counted into bins?

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life."* A histogram
answers the same question; here `line` replaces `bar`, and `density` replaces
`bin`.

How did life expectancy change across the decades in the five Asian countries
of `gapminder_asia`, one line per country?

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country."*
`color` does two things here. It splits the rows into one line per country,
then gives each line its own color, exactly as it did in Reading practice.

Do richer countries also live longer inside each continent, one panel per
continent?

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) | facet(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split
into panel columns by continent."* The `|` operator and `facet` split the
plot into panels. All the panels share one pair of scales, so they can be
compared; `free = TRUE` in a position gives each panel its own axis
([Faceting](faceting.qmd)).

Are the species apart when you see all three iris measurements together?

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is
petal length, color by species."* This is the 3-D plot from the end of Reading
practice, and this time you wrote it yourself.

## When gog says no {#when-gog-says-no}

Every sentence so far was correct. The other half of writing is what happens
when one is not.

You will write wrong sentences. Everyone does. gog promises that a wrong
sentence is refused with a message that says how to fix it, never drawn with
the wrong part quietly removed. Here are five refusals that new users see
most often.

Forgetting to bind the table. A sentence starts with `data()`, which names
the table:

```{r}
#| error: true
gapminder_2007 + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

The message above is R's. Python, Julia and JavaScript give the same advice,
each writing a column the way that language does.

Quoting a column name, a habit from other packages. The refusal names the
fix:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")
```

That message is R's too. Python and JavaScript name the fix `x(col.gdp)`, and
Julia names it `x(:gdp)`.

Mapping a channel to a column of the wrong type. `size` needs a continuous column,
because it shows an amount, and `continent` is a categorical column, so the
message suggests `color` or `shape` instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)
```

Forgetting the column a summary reads. The refusal names the missing `y`,
because `mean` must be told which column to average:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent)
```

Binning a category. `bin` divides a continuous axis into intervals, and the refusal names
`count`, the transform that tallies rows per category:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)
```

Each message names the rule and the fix. No wrong plot was drawn, and no binding
was dropped to complete one. Read any refusal outside this list the same way.

The last three refusals end with a second option: set `GOG_STRICT=0` and draw
the plot anyway. The first two are caught by the language's package before the
engine sees the sentence, so there is nothing to draw. `GOG_STRICT` is an environment variable, and [Drawing it
anyway](design-laws.qmd#drawing-it-anyway) shows which refusals `GOG_STRICT`
affects, with the one line that sets it in each language. For now, make the
fix the message asks for. At this stage, reading a refusal and making its fix
is the practice.

## The morning checkpoint {#the-morning-checkpoint}

That is the whole method: start with the minimum sentence, look, refine, and read
the refusal when one comes. If you have read this part from the start, check
yourself against the three skills [A morning](parts/morning.qmd) promised:

- Read any gog sentence aloud before looking at its plot.
- Given a question (*distribution? comparison? relationship? change over
  time?*), write a sentence that answers it.
- Predict whether gog will draw a sentence or refuse it, and roughly what the
  refusal will say.

If you can do most of that, you have done what Part I set out to teach. You can read the
next part in order, or go directly to [the cookbook](cookbook/one-variable.qmd)
and answer your own questions, following a link back whenever a recipe uses a
word you want explained.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

Part I taught how a sentence is built. It did not show everything a single word
can do; Part II gives each kind of word chapters of its own. Its first chapter,
[Data](data.qmd), covers the table every sentence starts from: the shape gog
needs, and how gog reads each column's type.
